power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS).

Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM 2.5 or wildfire-related PM 2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM 2.5 exposure.
This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM 2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024.
This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates.
The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R² of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively.
Elevated total PM 2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS.

Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM 2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM 2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023.

Wildfire-related PM 2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM 2.5 -attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019).

These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM 2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

Fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) is associated with many adverse health outcomes, such as lung cancer, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases. [1] [2] [3] [4] The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) ranked PM 2.5 as the third leading risk factors globally in 2023. 5 Therefore, accurately quantifying population exposure to PM 2.5 at high spatial and temporal resolution is essential for assessing exposure disparities and associated health burdens.

text.text: Higher spatial resolution can substantially reduce exposure misclassification in health risk assessment and environmental epidemiological studies.
Higher temporal resolution can also help identify short-term peak exposures that would be obscured in annual averages.

Due to stringent regulation of anthropogenic emissions in the United States (U.S.), ambient PM 2.5 concentrations have shown an overall decreasing trend over the past two decades. 6 However, increasingly severe wildfire events in recent years have dramatically elevated short-term PM 2.5 exposure at the daily scale. 7 Such episodic pollution events cannot be adequately captured by annual average estimates.

text.text: Previous studies have applied machine learning (ML) algorithms to estimate high-resolution ambient ground-level PM 2.5 concentrations in the U.S. As one of the pioneering and most widely cited studies, Di et al. developed an ensemble model combining random forest, gradient boosting, and neural networks to estimate daily average PM 2.5 concentrations at 1-km spatial resolution across the contiguous United States (CONUS) from 2000 to 2015. 8 Their model incorporated satellite-derived aerosol optical depth (AOD), chemical transport model (CTM) simulations, meteorological variables, and land-use characteristics as predictors. 8 Subsequent studies have adopted similar frameworks to estimate 1-km daily PM 2.5 concentrations across the U.S. for different periods, using slightly different predictor sets and ML algorithms, such as deep forest and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] However, most existing studies either focused on periods before 2020 or trained models over long historical timeframes starting in the early 2000s, when ambient PM 2.5 concentrations were primarily driven by anthropogenic emissions. [8] [9] [10] [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] In contrast, few studies have specifically focused on the most recent decade with substantial wildfire smoke impacts in the U.S. 11, 20 Among the studies covering these wildfire-influenced years, Wei et al. developed a global model, which may not fully capture U.S.-specific emission patterns, regulatory environments, and wildfire characteristics. 20 Moreover, few studies explicitly incorporated wildfire-related predictors to characterize the complex relationships between wildfire activity and PM 2.5 concentrations. 14, 16, 21 As wildfire smoke has become the major driver of ambient PM 2.5 in U.S. recently, many studies have attempted to apportion total PM 2.5 concentrations to wildfire and non-wildfire sources.

text.text: The first type of studies has relied on fire contributions simulated by CTMs.

Some of these studies directly derived wildfire-attributable PM 2.5 using CTMs with fire emission inventories, 22, 23 while others first obtained the proportion of CTM-based wildfire PM 2.5 in CTM-based total PM 2.5 and then applied the proportion to total PM 2.5 concentrations predicted from ML models. 24, 25 Although these CTM-based approaches offer strong physical interpretability, they may introduce substantial uncertainty in wildfire attribution due to uncertainties in fire emission inventories and CTM simulations, as the attribution is not directly constrained by ground-level observations.

text.text: As a complement to CTM-based approaches, the second type of studies has leveraged statistical approaches to partition wildfire and non-wildfire air pollutants based on ground-level and satellite-based data sources. 7, 16, [26] [27] [28] [29] One widely used statistical approach, developed by Burke et al., integrated ground-level PM 2.5 measurements with smoke plume data to estimate the difference between observed total PM 2.5 and counterfactual non-wildfire PM 2.5 concentrations. 7 This framework was further extended by Childs et al., who incorporated these wildfire PM 2.5 estimates into a ML model to produce 10-km daily estimates of wildfire PM 2.5 concentrations across the CONUS. 28 Although the smoke plume boundaries drawn by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) analysts used in this approach may lead to bias in wildfire attribution, this approach has been well validated against ground-level observations and can be extended to large spatial scales due to relatively low computation costs. 28 Nevertheless, a gap remains in the proportion of wildfire PM 2.5 in total PM 2.5 across the U.S., 16 particularly during recent wildfire-dominated years.

text.text: To address these critical gaps in recent wildfire-era exposure characterization, this study focuses on the wildfire-influenced period after 2018 and incorporates wildfire-related predictors into a machine learning framework.

Specifically, the objectives of this study are to (1) provide accurate 1-km daily estimates of ambient PM 2.5 concentrations across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024; (2) estimate 1-km daily wildfire-related PM 2.5 concentrations and their annual contribution to total PM 2.5 ; and (3) quantify county-level long-term mortality burdens attributable to both total and wildfire PM 2.5.
Data were collected across the CONUS between 2018 and 2024 from multiple sources.

Hourly ground-level PM 2.5 mass concentrations were obtained from the Air Quality System (AQS) operated by United States Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA), with a total of 1013 regulatory monitoring stations across the CONUS. 30 To improve our ML model performance, a series of relevant and available features were selected, including aerosol optical depth (AOD), atmospheric precursor concentrations, meteorological variables, population, economy level, land-use variables, and wildfire indicator.

text.text: AOD has been successfully used to predict ambient PM 2.5 , and is commonly used in ML-based PM 2.5 studies.

Satellite AOD at 550 nm was retrieved from the Multi-angle Implementation of Atmospheric Correction (MAIAC) AOD product (MCD19A2), which combined Terra and Aqua Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) products and had a 1-km resolution. 31 To address missing values of the satellite AOD product (e.g., cloud coverage), additional gap-free modeled hourly AOD product was used from Goddard Earth Observing System composition forecast (GEOS-CF) in 0.25° 0.25° resolution (method for imputation of missing 1-km satellite AOD described in Section 2.2). 32 In addition, simulated ground-level PM 2.5 concentrations were extracted from the GEOS-CF model (0.25° 0.25°, hourly). 32 The GEOS-CF product also provided the simulated concentrations of multiple other atmospheric PM 2.5 precursors, including ammonia (NH 3 ), nitrogen oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ), formaldehyde, benzene, toluene, xylenes, and isoprene. 32 We also included anthropogenic emission of monoterpenes and non-methane volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) global dataset (0.1° 0.1°, monthly) to capture the possible impact of other precursors.

text.text: 33     Meteorological conditions and their vertical profiles are also vital in predicting ambient PM 2.5 concentrations with high spatiotemporal resolution.

Therefore, we included temperature, dewpoint temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, northward and eastward components of wind speed, evaporation, surface pressure, and boundary layer height (BLH) from ERA5-Land (0.1° 0.1°, hourly) and ERA5 (0.25° 0.25°, hourly) reanalysis datasets. 34, 35 Since the CONUS experienced severe wildfire events during the study period (2018-2024), we obtained wildfire smoke density (polygon, daily) from NOAA's Hazard Mapping System (HMS) smoke product. 36 Four levels of smoke density are reported in the HMS dataset, including none, light, medium, and heavy smoke.

We collected WorldPop population (1 km, annual) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) nighttime lights (500m, monthly). 37, 38 We also considered several land-use variables as proxies of local emissions, including normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) from MOD13A3 (1 km, monthly), 39 percentage of 16 land cover types from National Land Cover Database (NLCD, 30 m, annual), 40 road density using all roads from Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing (TIGER) database (annual). 41 In addition, elevation data were obtained from Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM, 90 m). 42 All hourly data were aggregated to daily average using UTC time zone for consistency across the CONUS.

text.text: And all raster data were projected onto a predefined 1-km resolution grid covering the CONUS using the NAD83 / CONUS Albers Equal Area Conic projection coordinated system (EPSG:5070).

As other studies have previously described, total PM 2.5 prediction was developed using a four-dimensional space-time extremely randomized trees (4D-STET) model. 20, 43 Extremely randomized trees (extra-trees) is a tree-based ensemble learning algorithm, which introduces additional randomness in split selection, thereby improving robustness to noisy data and highly correlated predictors compared with the random forest model.

text.text: The "four-dimensional space-time" framework incorporates the Euclidean spherical spatial coordinates and triangular spiral temporal representations to account for spatiotemporal heterogeneity.

To address the missingness of satellite AOD data, we adopted a two-stage modeling strategy. 20 The first stage fit the 4D-STET model to fill the AOD gaps using simulated AOD from GEOS-CF, selected meteorological data, NDVI, elevation, and spatiotemporal terms.
text.formatted: To address the missingness of satellite AOD data, we adopted a two-stage modeling strategy. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> The first stage fit the 4D-STET model to fill the AOD gaps using simulated AOD from GEOS-CF, selected meteorological data, NDVI, elevation, and spatiotemporal terms.

text.text: Then the second stage applied the 4D-STET model with the gap-filled AOD, all meteorological data, population, nighttime lights, all land-use variables, and wildfire smoke density to predict ground-level daily average total PM 2.5 concentrations.
The hyperparameters in the two 4D-STET models were carefully tuned based on minimizing the out-of-bag (OOB) errors.
Details about model structures and hyperparameter tuning are available in SI Section S1.
With the optimal hyperparameters, the final 4D-STET model was used to predict the daily average total PM 2.5 concentrations at each grid across the CONUS and in each day between 2018 and 2024.
The final 4D-STET model of ground-level total PM 2.5 was evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation (CV) approaches.

Three CV strategies were applied: Sample-based CV, station-based CV, and day-based CV. 20 Specifically, all data samples, regulatory monitoring stations, or days were randomly divided into ten folds separately, with nine folds used for training and the remaining one for validation.

text.text: This procedure was repeated ten times so that each fold served as the validation dataset once.

Although sample-based CV was most commonly used in previous ML-based studies, the assumption of independent samples in sample-based CV was likely violated for spatiotemporally correlated PM 2.5 data in this study, which potentially resulted in data leakage and overly optimistic estimates of model performance.
In contrast, station-based and day-based CV can account for spatial and temporal autocorrelation within the dataset and evaluate model generalizability from both spatial and temporal perspectives.
Spatial generalization was particularly important because the regulatory monitoring stations were not evenly distributed across CONUS.

We pooled the observations and predictions from validation datasets in ten runs, and then calculated a series of out-of-sample evaluation metrics, including the coefficient of determination (R² ), root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), mean bias error (MBE), and normalized RMSE (NRMSE, defined as RMSE divided by the mean of all observations).

To evaluate monthly and annual averages of daily total PM 2.5 prediction, we also estimated the out-of-sample performance metrics of monthly and annual average predictions based on the above pooled daily CV results, using grid-months and grid-years with at least 80% of observations, respectively.

In addition to evaluating the model predictive performance, we examined model interpretability using the mean absolute SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values to quantify the relative contributions of individual features to PM 2.5 predictions.

44, 45 Partial dependence plots (PDPs) were further generated for selected features ranking among the highest according to their mean absolute SHAP values, in order to characterize the marginal relationships between total PM 2.5 levels and individual features. 46

This study provides high-resolution estimates of total and wildfire-related PM 2.5 concentrations across the CONUS during recent wildfire-influenced years and highlights the growing role of wildfire smoke in shaping PM 2.5 exposure patterns.

Our results suggest that while the U.S. west coast experienced the most severe episodic pollution events, elevated total PM 2.5 concentrations were also observed in several metropolitan areas across both western and eastern regions.

The contribution of wildfire smoke to total PM 2.5 was over 30% during major wildfire years in the west coast and over 20% during long-range smoke transport events in the east coast, highlighting the increasing influence of climate-driven wildfire activity on air quality.

Consistent with these exposure patterns, the mortality burden attributable to wildfire-related PM 2.5 also showed considerable interannual variability, underscoring the growing public health importance of wildfire smoke in the U.S.

text.text: Since exposure and health risk assessments primarily depend on the accuracy of absolute exposure estimates, RMSE was considered as the primary CV metric.
However, as different studies covered different time periods with quite different total PM 2.5 concentrations, NRMSE provides a more appropriate basis for comparison.
The sample-based CV NRMSE at the daily scale in this study was 0.38 across the CONUS, which was similar to values reported by Wei et al.
(0.40; CONUS, 2000-2020) 15 and Kayastha et al.
11 The sample-based CV NRMSEs in the Mountain and Pacific Divisions reached 0.45 and 0.47, respectively, which were lower than that reported by Reid et al.
12 Similar patterns were observed for station-based CV.
Notably, the comparable or improved performance in this study was achieved under more challenging modeling conditions.

For example, Wei et al. and Reid et al. covered the early 2000s with higher total PM 2.5 concentrations which may be easier to predict due to stronger signal-to-noise ratios; 12, 15 and Kayastha et al. developed predictions at a coarser 4-km spatial resolution instead of 1-km resolution.
Many previous studies did not report NRMSE values, but instead reported CV R² , which we considered as our secondary evaluation metric.

text.text: As a global chemical transport modeling system, GEOS-CF provides spatially and temporally complete, process-based estimates that integrate information on emissions, atmospheric chemistry, transport, deposition, and meteorological conditions.
It therefore served as a baseline estimate of regional and temporal PM 2.5 variation for the ML model.

A conceptually similar modeling strategy has been used in previous studies, in which spatially interpolated regulatory monitoring observations provided an observation-based baseline estimate for subsequent ML prediction. 52 Compared with interpolation based primarily on the geographic configuration and AQS monitoring data, the GEOS-CF field can represent pollution transport and chemical processes across areas with sparse monitoring coverage.

text.text: This can be interpreted by secondary aerosol formation mechanisms.

Ammonia is one of the most important precursors to PM 2.5 and plays a vital role in the formation of secondary inorganic aerosols (SIAs), such as ammonium nitrate (NH 4 NO 3 ) and ammonium sulfate ((NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 ). text.text: The high-resolution mapping of PM 2.5 concentrations is critical for reducing possible exposure misclassification.

Many EPA regulatory monitoring stations are located far away from the local sources, so using the nearest EPA regulatory monitoring data or their spatial interpolations, such as inverse distance weighting and kriging, may not adequately capture the impact of emission sources on PM 2.5 concentrations in those areas without regulatory monitoring.
Machine learning models could address this limitation by incorporating many source-related predictors, such as road density and emission inventories.

Some widely used PM 2.5 products are available only at relatively coarse spatial resolutions (e.g., 10 km and 12 km). 88, 89 To evaluate the impact of spatial resolution, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by aggregating our 1-km estimates into a 10-km resolution.

text.text: In addition to high spatial resolution, this study also predicted PM 2.5 at a high temporal resolution, i.e., daily averages, which can further reduce exposure misclassification associated with temporal averaging.

Although annual average estimates are very useful for long-term health risk assessment, annual averages may obscure substantial day-to-day variations in PM 2.5 concentrations, particularly in those regions influenced by mask short-term episodic pollution such as wildfire smoke.

In contrast, daily exposure estimates can better characterize exposure dynamics, capture peak exposure metrics in addition to long-term cumulative exposure, and facilitate future epidemiological studies about short-term health effects.
Furthermore, the daily estimates can enable the separation of wildfire and non-wildfire PM 2.5 contributions.
Although many PM 2.5 models have been developed in previous studies, relatively few distinguish between wildfire and non-wildfire contributions.

This separation is essential because the two sources typically exhibit distinct temporal patterns and potentially different exposure-response relationships, thus possibly contributing disproportionately to short-term health risks.

Previous studies have suggested that short-term exposure to wildfire-related PM 2.5 may have much stronger respiratory health effects than non-wildfire PM 2.5 exposure. 90, 91 Future epidemiological studies can also rely on this separation to examine the associations between wildfire PM 2.5 and more health outcomes.

While county-level patterns generally follow fire geography, spatially aggregated division-level estimates exhibited different patterns after considering population weighting.
Since severe wildfire smoke hit both western and eastern U.S. in 2021, we use this year as an illustrative example.
The average concentration of wildfire PM 2.5 in Pacific Division (2.31 μg/m 3 ) was higher than that in Middle Atlantic (0.77 μg/m 3 ) and West North Central (1.55 μg/m 3 ) Divisions.

However, the population-weighted average exposure of wildfire PM 2.5 in Pacific Division (0.82 μg/m 3 ) was comparable to that in Middle Atlantic Division (0.84 μg/m 3 ) and substantially lower than that in West North Central Division (1.43 μg/m 3 ).

Consistent with these exposure patterns, the mortality rate due to wildfire PM 2.5 in Pacific Division in 2021 (5.98 deaths per 100,000) was similar to that in Middle Atlantic Division (5.85) and much lower than West North Central Division (10.77).

When averaged over 2018-2024, the highest wildfire-attributable mortality rates were observed in West North Central (6.80 deaths per 100,000) and East South Central (6.69) Divisions, rather than in Pacific Division (4.68 ).
These findings highlight that the health impacts of wildfire smoke in recent years were comparable between eastern and western U.S. regions when evaluated from a population exposure perspective.
This suggests that wildfire smoke should be considered a nationwide public health concern rather than solely a western U.S.
environmental issue, and that public awareness and preparedness for wildfire smoke events should be strengthened across the entire country.

text.text: Emission control strategies are highly effective for reducing anthropogenic PM 2.5 , while preventive measures to mitigate exposure should be emphasized for wildfire PM 2.5 .
During severe wildfire smoke events, individuals are advised to stay indoors and limit outdoor activities.

Keeping windows closed and using portable air cleaners with HEPA filters can further reduce indoor exposure. 96 When outdoor activities are unavoidable, wearing properly fitted N95 or equivalent respirators is strongly recommended.

text.text: In addition, smoke forecasting and early warning systems should be strengthened by local governments to improve risk communication and enhance public health preparedness.
This study has several strengths.

First, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to predict 1-km daily average concentrations of both total and wildfire-related PM 2.5 across the CONUS with a focus on recent wildfire-influenced years.

Many previous studies have covered long timeframes beginning in the early 2000s, during which anthropogenic emissions, rather than wildfire events, were the primary drivers of total PM 2.5 variability.
By contrast, our study focused on the 2018-2024 period, when wildfire activity increasingly dominated interannual variability in total PM 2.5 concentrations.
Second, our machine learning framework incorporated predictors specifically relevant to wildfire and atmospheric chemistry.
We included wildfire smoke, which many previous studies have not done.
This focus allows for a clearer characterization of the growing influence of wildfire smoke on air quality under substantially reduced anthropogenic emissions.

We also incorporated multiple chemically relevant precursor species from the GEOS-CF model, including key gaseous pollutants associated with secondary PM 2.5 formation, which helped improve model performance and better capture the chemical processes influencing PM 2.5 variability.

Third, few studies have simultaneously estimated the total and wildfire-related PM 2.5 concentrations during recent wildfire-influenced years, which is essential for quantifying the contribution of wildfire smoke to total PM 2.5 exposure.
Future epidemiological studies can use this distinction between wildfire and non-wildfire PM 2.5 to examine source-specific health effects.

Fourth, this study provided a comprehensive evaluation of model performance, including sample-, station-, and day-based CV metrics (i.e., R² , RMSE, MAE, MBE, and NRMSE) for daily, monthly, and annual average estimates, whereas previous studies only reported a more limited set of these metrics, making direct inter-study comparison challenging.

Finally, our framework relied entirely on publicly accessible data sources, facilitating future updates and extensions, and we released the resulting prediction datasets to support further research on total and wildfire PM 2.5 exposure and its health impacts.
However, several limitations should also be noted.

First, the cross-validation results suggest that our model slightly underestimated extremely high total PM 2.5 concentrations during wildfire episodes, a limitation also reported in previous ML-based PM 2.5 prediction studies.
Possible reasons include the relatively low frequency of episodic wildfire events, the use of mean squared error as the loss function, and the leaf-averaging effect in tree-based models.
In addition, uncertainties in the HMS smoke product may affect the model's ability to characterize wildfire-related PM 2.5 .
Because HMS smoke polygons rely largely on daytime visible satellite imagery, they may fail to detect smaller or lower-intensity smoke plumes, including those from some prescribed fires.

Furthermore, the two-dimensional smoke polygons provide limited information on plume altitude and therefore cannot reliably distinguish elevated smoke plumes from smoke that reaches the surface and contributes to ground-level PM 2.5 concentrations.
Second, the proportional PAF approach was used in this study to separate the health impacts from wildfire-related and non-wildfire PM 2.5 .

Although it ensures that the sum of source-specific health burdens equals the total attributable burden, it assumes that wildfire-related and non-wildfire PM 2.5 share the same exposure-response relationships with all-cause mortality.

While some studies have suggested potentially differentiated health effects of wildfire-related PM 2.5 , 95 more epidemiological evidence is required to better characterize source-specific health risks.
Third, this study only focused on the long-term health impacts of total and wildfire-related PM 2.5 .
Future studies could further investigate short-term health impacts, especially those associated with episodic wildfire-related PM 2.5 peak exposures.
This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM 2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024.
The model had a good predictive performance and revealed substantial spatiotemporal variability in total PM 2.5 pollution during recent wildfire-influenced years.
The U.S. west coast experienced the most severe episodic pollution events, while many metropolitan areas across both western and eastern regions had considerable numbers of highly polluted days.

Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM 2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 30-35% of total PM 2.5 along the west coast during 2020-2021, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023.
In severe wildfire years, wildfire smoke also contributed over 20% of population exposure in both western and eastern regions, highlighting its growing influence on air quality nationwide.

For long-term health impacts, the mortality burden attributable to total PM 2.5 peaked in 2021 (62.7 per 100,000), while wildfire-related PM 2.5 mortality was highest in 2023 (10.23 per 100,000), accounting for 18.4% of total PM 2.5 -related deaths.

Notably, when evaluated from a population exposure perspective, the health impacts of wildfire smoke were comparable between eastern and western U.S. regions, underscoring the importance of recognizing wildfire smoke as a nationwide public health concern rather than a regionally confined issue. 1243  1255 (a) 1256
